title: Build a `Map<String, BigDecimal>` of account id to total balance from a stream of transactions where the same account appears multiple times, using `Collectors.toMap` with a merge function. Explain the `IllegalStateException` on duplicate keys and how the merge function resolves it.
shortTitle: Build an account-to-balance map with Collectors.toMap and resolve duplicate keys with a merge function
keyPoints: A stream of transactions has many rows per account, so the account id is a duplicate key when collected with `toMap`.
The two-argument `toMap` throws `IllegalStateException` on the first duplicate key instead of overwriting silently.
The merge function `(existing, incoming) -> existing.add(incoming)` sums balances instead of discarding one.
Money must be summed with `BigDecimal.add`, never with `double`, to avoid floating-point rounding errors.
`Collectors.groupingBy` with `Collectors.reducing`/`summingX` is an alternative when every key naturally maps to many rows.
The merge function must be associative so the result is correct for parallel streams.

s1_definition.oneliner: `toMap(Transaction::getAccountId, Transaction::getAmount, BigDecimal::add)` builds account id to total balance, and the merge function `BigDecimal::add` sums the amounts of transactions that share an account.
s1_definition.profdef:
`Collectors.toMap` with a merge function aggregates a stream into a `Map` even when keys repeat.

- **Key mapper** – extracts the grouping key, here the account id.
- **Value mapper** – extracts the value to aggregate, here the transaction amount as `BigDecimal`.
- **Merge function** – a `BinaryOperator` invoked when two values share a key; `BigDecimal::add` sums them.
- **IllegalStateException** – thrown by the two-argument form on the first duplicate key, because it has no rule to combine values.

Supplying the merge function turns a collision from a crash into a running total.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, Priya receives a pile of transaction slips, many for the same account. She wants one line per account showing the total balance. Without a rule, when a second slip for the same account appears she stops and raises her hand, because she cannot put two amounts in one box: that is the `IllegalStateException`. The merge function is the written instruction "add the new amount to the amount already recorded," which lets her keep a running total per account instead of freezing.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Stream<Transaction>
   (ACC-1, 1000.00)
   (ACC-2,  500.00)
   (ACC-1,  250.00)   <- duplicate key ACC-1
        │
        │  toMap(getAccountId, getAmount, MERGE)
        ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              Collectors.toMap                    │
  │  put ACC-1 -> 1000.00                             │
  │  put ACC-2 ->  500.00                             │
  │  ACC-1 again?                                     │
  │     no MERGE  ──▶ IllegalStateException(ACC-1)    │
  │     MERGE = BigDecimal::add                        │
  │         existing 1000.00 + incoming 250.00         │
  │         = 1250.00                                  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
  Map<String, BigDecimal>
   { ACC-1 = 1250.00, ACC-2 = 500.00 }
```

```text
  Why BigDecimal for money
  double :  0.10 + 0.20 = 0.30000000000000004   (drift)
  BigDecimal: 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.30                 (exact)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When Priya builds a `Map<String, BigDecimal>` of account id to total balance from a transaction stream, the key insight is that a transaction log has many rows per account. The account id is therefore a duplicate key, and the two-argument `Collectors.toMap` treats the first duplicate as an error. It throws `IllegalStateException` naming both amounts, because it has no rule for putting two values in one box, the same way Priya raises her hand when she cannot file two slips under one account.

The fix is the three-argument `toMap` with a merge function. The merge runs only on a collision and receives the balance already recorded and the incoming amount. Returning `existing.add(incoming)`, written as `BigDecimal::add`, turns the collision into a running total. Now each account appears once with the sum of all its transactions.

Money makes the type choice non-negotiable. `double` cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly, so summing balances as `double` drifts, and `0.10 + 0.20` prints as `0.30000000000000004`. `BigDecimal` stores digits exactly and `add` is precise, which is why every amount stays a `BigDecimal` through the whole pipeline.

There is an alternative. `groupingBy` with `reducing` or `summingX` totals balances too, and reads more naturally when the mental model is "group the rows, then combine each group." Choose `toMap` with a merge when you want one explicit aggregate per key, and `groupingBy` when grouping is the dominant idea or you need several downstream aggregations.

In our banking work the discipline is clear: expect duplicate keys in any transaction feed, supply `BigDecimal::add` as the merge, and never let money touch `double`.

Remember one sentence: a transaction stream has duplicate account ids, so give `toMap` a `BigDecimal::add` merge function to sum balances instead of crashing with `IllegalStateException`.
